final_proof:
Let
\[
C(I)=\{f:I\to\mathbb R: f\text{ is continuous}\}.
\]
For \(f,g\in C(I)\), \(c\in\mathbb R\), and \(x\in I\), define
\[
(f+g)(x)=f(x)+g(x),\qquad (c\cdot f)(x)=c f(x).
\]

First these operations are closed on \(C(I)\). If \(f,g\in C(I)\), then the sum theorem for continuous real-valued functions says that \(f+g\) is continuous on \(I\). If \(c\in\mathbb R\) and \(f\in C(I)\), the constant function \(x\mapsto c\) is continuous on \(I\), so the product theorem for continuous functions shows that \(c\cdot f\) is continuous on \(I\). Thus pointwise addition is a map \(C(I)\times C(I)\to C(I)\), and pointwise scalar multiplication is a map \(\mathbb R\times C(I)\to C(I)\).

We now verify the vector-space axioms. Let \(f,g,h\in C(I)\), let \(r,s\in\mathbb R\), and let \(x\in I\). The associative and commutative laws for addition in \(\mathbb R\) give
\[
((f+g)+h)(x)=(f(x)+g(x))+h(x)=f(x)+(g(x)+h(x))=(f+(g+h))(x)
\]
and
\[
(f+g)(x)=f(x)+g(x)=g(x)+f(x)=(g+f)(x).
\]
Define \(0_I:I\to\mathbb R\) by \(0_I(x)=0\). It is continuous, hence belongs to \(C(I)\), and
\[
(f+0_I)(x)=f(x)+0=f(x).
\]
Define \((-f):I\to\mathbb R\) by \((-f)(x)=-f(x)\). This is \((-1)\cdot f\), so it belongs to \(C(I)\), and
\[
(f+(-f))(x)=f(x)-f(x)=0=0_I(x).
\]
Thus \(C(I)\) is an abelian group under pointwise addition.

The field laws in \(\mathbb R\) also give
\[
((rs)\cdot f)(x)=(rs)f(x)=r(sf(x))=(r\cdot(s\cdot f))(x),
\]
\[
(1\cdot f)(x)=1f(x)=f(x),
\]
\[
(r\cdot(f+g))(x)=r(f(x)+g(x))=rf(x)+rg(x)=((r\cdot f)+(r\cdot g))(x),
\]
and
\[
((r+s)\cdot f)(x)=(r+s)f(x)=rf(x)+sf(x)=((r\cdot f)+(s\cdot f))(x).
\]
Each displayed equality holds for every \(x\in I\); by extensionality of functions, the corresponding functions are equal. Consequently all vector-space axioms over \(\mathbb R\) hold, and therefore \(\bigl(C(I),+,\cdot\bigr)\) is a real vector space.
